title: Europe's Biggest Bat Hunts Songbirds in the Dark, a Kilometre Up

scenes.text: Songbirds migrate at night to avoid hawks. Something else is waiting.
For nearly 25 years, scientists kept finding bird feathers in the droppings of Europe's largest bat. Nobody knew how they got there.
So in Spain they strapped tiny recorders to greater noctule bats. One climbed more than a kilometre and locked on to a robin.
It dived after the bird for nearly three minutes. The microphone caught the robin's distress calls. Then they stopped.
What followed was 23 minutes of chewing, in mid-air. The bat bites off the wings and eats as it flies, using the skin between its legs as a pouch.
The night sky was never the safe route. It just had a different hunter.

description:
Songbirds migrate at night to avoid daytime predators, but Europe's largest bat, the greater noctule, hunts them more than a kilometre above the ground.
Recorders strapped to 14 bats in Spain captured one chasing a robin in a dive of nearly three minutes, then 23 minutes of chewing in flight. The study, published in Science in 2025, solved a puzzle that began nearly 25 years earlier with feathers in bat droppings.
Did you know any bat could catch a bird in flight?
subject: greater noctule bat
first_comment: The same bats usually hunt insects only about 53 metres up. For birds they climb twenty times higher. Which night hunter should we cover next?
